title: Multiple-choice questions
subtitle: Longer text, two answers, and the writer's purpose
summary: Read across several connected sentences to answer a multiple-choice question, pick two answers from five, and work out why the writer wrote a paragraph at all.

lesson.heading: The answer is spread over several sentences
lesson.text: A multiple-choice question rarely sits on one line. You usually have to read **two or more connected sentences** and put them together. Read the extract quickly for the main point, then go back and read it carefully.

examples.text: *Linguists agree that language is needed during reading, **but at which stage** language becomes a necessity **has come under debate**.*
examples.note: This is the disagreement - so the answer is *when our language ability begins to affect reading ability*.

examples.text: *Past research has shown that animals have the ability to discriminate letters ...*
examples.note: True, but it is not what linguists disagree about.

examples.text: *Findings recently published in the journal Science challenge this long-held notion ...*
examples.note: Also true, and also not the disagreement.

lesson.note: Look for the words that name a disagreement - *debate*, *challenge*, *dispute*, *contrary to* - when the question asks what people differ on.

left.label: A direct question
examples: *According to the paragraph, what point do linguists have different views on?*
Each option is a complete idea.

right.label: An incomplete sentence
examples: *According to the second paragraph, the Garden City Movement ...*
The grammar must fit as well as the meaning.

lesson.heading: Choosing TWO answers from five
lesson.text: Some questions ask for **two** correct answers out of five. You have to read and weigh even more text, so highlight the parts of the passage that introduce a first and a second idea, then test each option against them.

examples.text: *there were probably **several related phenomena** ... **Firstly**, ... Something else was going on. That something was distinctively **human**.*
examples.note: Those three signals mark the two issues.

examples.text: **B** *Female dolphins were able to breed earlier than usual.* - correct
examples.note: *After a female dolphin loses her calf, she can give birth again much sooner.*

examples.text: **E** *The dolphins had less contact with humans after the hurricane.* - correct
examples.note: Fewer boats meant more time eating and less time avoiding them.

examples.text: **A** *More female dolphins survived than males.* - wrong
**C** *The dolphins had access to greater numbers of shrimp and fish.* - wrong
examples.note: The catch brought to shore fell; the passage credits the change to fewer boats, not to more fish.

lesson.heading: Questions about the writer's purpose
lesson.text: Some questions ask why the writer made a particular reference, what the purpose of a part of the text is, or what the writer's opinion is. For these you must look past the surface meaning of the words to the writer's **tone**.

examples.note: It describes a film that is very popular.
It criticises the science portrayed in the film.
It gives a positive image of people enjoying the film.

lesson.note: A writer who uses two warm words and one cold one is usually saying *this was wrong, and it did not matter*.

lesson.heading: Purpose and opinion on the same paragraph
rows: To argue that people may choose to believe the improbable in order to be entertained
The writer says we are happy to *suspend our disbelief*
What is the writer's opinion of *Jurassic Park*?
In spite of its inaccuracies, it was a successful novel and film
The science is *hopelessly flawed*, but the book was *successful* and the film a *blockbuster*

lesson.text: Try covering the options and answering the question in your own words first. Then look for the option that says what you said - it is much harder for a well-written distractor to pull you off an answer you have already formed.

exercises.prompt: *Linguists agree that language is needed during reading, but at which stage language becomes a necessity has come under debate.* What do linguists have different views on?
options: Whether animals are intelligent enough to learn to read
Whether reading ability is linked to writing ability
When our language ability begins to affect reading ability
When early humans developed the ability to read and write
exercises.explanation: *At which stage ... has come under debate* is the disagreement. The other options describe things the paragraph mentions but nobody argues about.

exercises.prompt: Does each word give the writer's tone a positive or a negative colour?

exercises.statement: A multiple-choice question can usually be answered from a single sentence of the passage.
exercises.explanation: You normally need two or more connected sentences - which is why the distractors so often match one sentence each.

exercises.prompt: The passage says the science in *Jurassic Park* is *hopelessly flawed* but the book was *successful* and the film a *blockbuster*. What is the writer's opinion of it?
options: The film was not a faithful rendition of the original book
It shows how important thorough research is for successful writers
In spite of its inaccuracies, it was a successful novel and film
It is a good example of the importance of science fact in science fiction
exercises.explanation: The criticism and the praise both have to be carried by the answer. The other options keep only one half.

exercises.prompt: The writer says the premise was science-ish enough to let us ___ our disbelief and enjoy the dinosaurs.
exercises.hint: (a verb meaning to hold something back)
exercises.explanation: *Suspend our disbelief* is the phrase that gives the purpose: people choose to believe the improbable to be entertained.

exercises.prompt: *In Mississippi, 87% of commercial fishing vessels were damaged, so the seafood brought into shore fell by nearly 15%.* Why is *The dolphins had access to greater numbers of shrimp and fish* a distractor?
options: Because no fish are mentioned in the passage
Because the passage credits the change to fewer boats, not to more fish
Because the percentages are the wrong way round
Because Miller did not study dolphins
exercises.explanation: The deduction the passage actually makes is that dolphins spent more time eating and less time avoiding boats.

exercises.statement: When a question asks you to choose TWO answers from five, you should expect to read more of the passage than for an ordinary multiple-choice question.
exercises.explanation: Two separate ideas have to be located and five options weighed, so budget the time accordingly.

exercises.prompt: Match each type of purpose question with what it asks you to find.

pairs.left: Why did the writer mention Miletus?
pairs.right: the reason for a particular reference

pairs.left: What is the purpose of the final paragraph?
pairs.right: the job a part of the text does

pairs.left: What is the writer's view of the film?

exercises.prompt: Build the phrase in the passage that marks the first of two related causes.
exercises.answer: there were probably several related phenomena that, combined, could explain the increase.
exercises.explanation: *Several ... combined* warns you that one cause on its own is not the answer.

exercises.prompt: What is the most useful thing to do before you read the four options?
options: Count how many words each option has
Answer the question in your own words first
Look for the option that repeats the most words from the passage
exercises.explanation: An answer you have already formed is much harder for a distractor to dislodge - and repeated words are usually the distractor's trick.
